title: Best Hearing Protection for Indoor Shooting Ranges: Earplugs, Earmuffs or Both?
summary: You clip a fresh target to the carrier, send it out to seven yards and settle into your stance. Two lanes over, another shooter starts working through a box of 9mm, and the sound of every one of those shots comes back at you off the concrete walls. By the end of your hour, your ears feel full and the drive home sounds a little muffled. That full, muffled feeling is a sign that the one layer of hearing protection you were wearing wasn't enough for a closed room. If you're choosing between earplugs and earmuffs, the best indoor range ear protection is both: earplugs seated under earmuffs. According to NIOSH, earmuffs alone cut peak gunshot noise by an average of 26 dB, while earmuffs worn over earplugs cut it by 44 dB. NIOSH recommends double protection at indoor firing ranges. Electronic earmuffs let you wear both layers of hearing protection and still hear range commands. If you're planning your first trip to the range, it's easier to start with both layers than to add one later. Outdoors, the sound blast from your firearm spreads out over open ground. Indoors, your range's concrete walls, ceiling, baffles, and lane dividers reflect that blast back toward the firing line. A gunshot is already over the noise safe limit before any reflection adds to it. NIOSH measured peak sound pressure levels of 155 to 168 dB SPL from law enforcement firearms during live fire. The limit for impulse noise is 140 dB peak, and OSHA's noise standard sets that same ceiling. Every 10 dB is ten times the sound energy, so a shot that lands 28 dB over the limit carries several hundred times the energy the limit allows. Reflected sound can reach your ears a fraction of a second after the direct sound. You hear your muzzle blast first, and then the room sends part of that blast sound back to you. Those same walls reflect the shots from every other lane too. A shooter three lanes down is firing into the same room you are, and you have no say over how many rounds that shooter fires. Muzzle brakes and compensators can make that sound worse at close range. A muzzle brake on a rifle or a compensator on a pistol vents gas out the sides of the muzzle. That side blast hits the lane dividers and pushes toward the shooters beside it, so a braked rifle at the bench next to you can be the loudest firearm you hear in your session. A lane rental often means an hour of steady fire, so your exposure keeps adding up long after shooting your first magazine. All of that reflected sound lands on your earplugs first. The next section shows why a single earplug can't handle it. Why Earplugs Alone Aren't Enough at an Indoor Range Earplugs alone aren't sufficient hearing protection on an indoor shooting range because a single layer can leave the loudest gunshots above the 140 dB peak limit. NIOSH measured an average peak reduction of 24 dB for earplugs alone. Against a 168 dB shot, that still leaves about 144 dB at your ear. NIOSH's case data shows how much a second layer adds: Setup Average peak reduction (NIOSH case data) A 168 dB shot at your ear Earplugs alone 24 dB About 144 dB, over the limit Earmuffs alone 26 dB About 142 dB, over the limit Earplugs under earmuffs 44 dB About 124 dB, under the limit The combined 44 dB is lower than the two layers added together, which would be 50 dB. One reason for this is that some sound reaches your inner ear through the bones of your skull, and no earplug or earmuff blocks that path. Even so, the second layer is what brings a 168 dB shot under the 140 dB limit. A higher-rated earplug won't close that gap by itself. The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) on your earplug packaging comes from lab testing with a careful fit. At the range, a rushed insertion or an ear tip in the wrong size can loosen the seal into your ear canal and cost you a large share of that rated protection. You can learn how NRR ratings work, and how to estimate your real-world protection, in our NRR guide. You'll see two ratings on AXIL products. NRR is the rating required on hearing protection sold in the United States. The Single Number Rating (SNR) comes from European testing, and a product's SNR usually reads a few decibels higher than its NRR. Compare NRR to NRR and SNR to SNR when you shop. For an indoor range, plan on wearing two layers of hearing protection. Earplugs under earmuffs will protect you better indoors than one device with a higher number on the box. Two passive layers give you that protection, but two passive layers also make range commands hard to hear. Electronic earmuffs solve that problem. Best Electronic Ear Protection for Indoor Shooting Ranges The best electronic ear protection for an indoor shooting range is a pair of electronic earmuffs worn over passive earplugs. That setup gives you NIOSH's recommended two layers of hearing protection and keeps range commands clear. With two passive layers on, it's hard to hear the range safety officer, a cease-fire call or the instructor standing behind you. When you can't hear a command, the natural move is to lift one earmuff cup. If someone fires while that cup is up, that ear is down to one layer of protection or none. Electronic earmuffs remove the reason to lift a cup. The microphones on your electronic earmuffs pick up speech and range commands and play them through the earmuff speakers. The earmuff circuit clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold, and your earplugs hold the seal underneath. When you compare electronic earmuffs for an indoor range, four features do most of the work: Feature Why it helps indoors What to look for Compression circuit Reflected gunshots arrive back to back from every lane A circuit that clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold Hear-through volume Your earplugs muffle speech under the cups Enough volume steps to make up for the earplug layer Low-profile cups Rifle stocks and bench positions crowd your earmuffs Slim cups that clear your cheek weld Runtime Lane sessions can run an hour or more, and range days run longer A full session or day on one charge or one set of batteries One thing to look out for is an electronic earmuff circuit's reaction speed. A slow circuit can let the start of each gunshot through before it clamps down. Electronic earbuds can also take the place of passive earplugs as your inner layer. Before a long session, check that your earbuds sit flush enough for your earmuff cushions to seal over them comfortably. An electronic setup only protects you as well as it fits. Seat your earplugs first, then put on your earmuffs, so the earmuff cushions close over your sealed ear canals. Tip: Roll your foam earplug tips tight, pull the top of your ear up and back, and hold each earplug in place for a few seconds while the foam expands. Shooting glasses with thin, flat arms let your earmuff cushions seal around the arms with a smaller gap. Tip: Put your glasses on before your earmuffs, then press each earmuff cushion flat against the glasses arm. A lane customer only needs that electronic setup to stay comfortable for an hour. Range safety officers and firearms instructors need the same setup to last the whole day. Hearing Protection for Range Safety Officers and Firearms Instructors Range safety officers and firearms instructors should consider wearing comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs that they can wear for every relay of the day. Your exposure is far higher than any customer's, so your hearing protection has to do more. A customer fires one session, while the person running the line hears every session, every day. Hearing damage from gunfire builds up across all of that exposure, which our article on shooter's ear explains in more detail. NIOSH reports that lead and noise at firing ranges can cause health problems, particularly among employees and instructors. Many firearms instructors also train law enforcement. On qualification day, a whole unit can cycle through your lanes, often with rifles and shotguns alongside pistols. NIOSH's double-protection recommendation applies to the instructor running that line as much as to the officers on it. For all-day wear, look for electronic earmuffs that run a full day on one charge, low-profile cups that stay comfortable for hours, and replaceable cushions for gear that sees heavy or shared use. Pair those earmuffs with an earplug you can wear for hours without noticing it. The MX PRO earmuffs run up to 70 hours in hearing enhancement mode, which covers several full range days between charges. Electronic hear-through lets you give commands and hear shooters' questions without lifting a cup. If radio communication is part of your job on the line, our comparison of tactical headsets and tactical earbuds covers the options built for that. Have a partner stand one lane away and call commands at normal volume, then raise your earmuff volume until you can follow every word. Setting the volume before shooting starts means you won't be reaching for a dial with a loaded firearm in your hand. At an outdoor range with a handgun, well-fitted earplugs may be enough for a short session. At an indoor range, NIOSH recommends earplugs and earmuffs together. Do noise cancelling headphones work at a gun range? Consumer noise cancelling headphones only count as hearing protection if they carry an NRR. If you need to hear someone, raise your earmuff volume instead of lifting a cup. When you're done shooting, wash up and wipe down your hearing protection before you eat. On the drive home, notice how your ears feel. If they feel full or sound muffled, your setup needs a better fit or another layer of protection before your next session. ## Indoor Ranges Reflect Every Gunshot Sound Back at You

All of that reflected sound lands on your earplugs first. The next section shows why a single earplug can't handle it.


## Why Earplugs Alone Aren't Enough at an Indoor Range


Earplugs alone aren't sufficient hearing protection on an indoor shooting range because a single layer can leave the loudest gunshots above the 140 dB peak limit. NIOSH measured an average peak reduction of 24 dB for earplugs alone. Against a 168 dB shot, that still leaves about 144 dB at your ear.

Earplugs alone 24 dB About 144 dB, over the limit


Earmuffs alone 26 dB About 142 dB, over the limit


Earplugs under earmuffs 44 dB About 124 dB, under the limit


The combined 44 dB is lower than the two layers added together, which would be 50 dB. One reason for this is that some sound reaches your inner ear through the bones of your skull, and no earplug or earmuff blocks that path. At the range, a rushed insertion or an ear tip in the wrong size can loosen the seal into your ear canal and cost you a large share of that rated protection. You can learn[how NRR ratings work, and how to estimate your real-world protection, in our NRR guide.](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/nrr-rating-for-shooting-everything-you-need-to-know-axil)

For an indoor range, plan on wearing two layers of hearing protection. Earplugs under earmuffs will protect you better indoors than one device with a higher number on the box.


Two passive layers give you that protection, but two passive layers also make range commands hard to hear. Electronic earmuffs solve that problem.


## Best Electronic Ear Protection for Indoor Shooting Ranges


The best electronic ear protection for an indoor shooting range is a pair of electronic earmuffs worn over passive earplugs. That setup gives you NIOSH's recommended two layers of hearing protection and keeps range commands clear.


With two passive layers on, it's hard to hear the range safety officer, a cease-fire call or the instructor standing behind you. When you can't hear a command, the natural move is to lift one earmuff cup. If someone fires while that cup is up, that ear is down to one layer of protection or none.


Electronic earmuffs remove the reason to lift a cup. The microphones on your electronic earmuffs pick up speech and range commands and play them through the earmuff speakers. The earmuff circuit clamps down the instant a gunshot crosses its threshold, and your earplugs hold the seal underneath. What NRR rating do you need for an indoor shooting range?


Wear two layers. Earplugs under earmuffs give you more protection indoors than any single device.


Are earplugs enough for the range?


At an outdoor range with a handgun, well-fitted earplugs may be enough for a short session. At an indoor range, NIOSH recommends earplugs and earmuffs together.


Do noise cancelling headphones work at a gun range?


Consumer noise cancelling headphones only count as hearing protection if they carry an NRR. Our article on[noise cancelling earbuds at the range](https://goaxil.com/blogs/axil/earbuds-at-the-shooting-range-why-noise-cancellation-cant-stop-the-sound-of-a-gunshot) explains why active noise cancellation can't stop the sound of a gunshot.


How loud is a gunshot indoors?


NIOSH measured peak levels of 155 to 168 dB SPL from law enforcement firearms. The limit for impulse noise is 140 dB peak.


Can you wear electronic earbuds under earmuffs?


Yes, electronic earbuds under earmuffs make a valid double-protection setup. Check that your earmuff cushions seal over the earbuds and that the fit stays comfortable for your full session.


Do gun ranges provide ear protection?


Most ranges rent or sell basic passive hearing protection. Bringing your own lets you choose the fit and add the second layer.


What should range safety officers and instructors wear?


Range safety officers and instructors should consider comfortable earplugs under long-runtime electronic earmuffs, so commands carry without anyone lifting a cup.


## A Simple Routine for Every Indoor Range Trip


The same short routine keeps both layers of your hearing protection working on every indoor range trip. If you're starting from one pair of earmuffs, begin with a pack of earplugs to wear under them. When you're ready to upgrade, electronic earmuffs let you hear the line without lifting a cup.


1. Before you leave your house, pack both layers of hearing protection with your range bag essentials, and charge your electronic earmuffs or pack spare batteries.
2. At your lane, seat your earplugs, put on your earmuffs and set your hear-through volume with a quick voice check.
3. On the firing line, leave both layers on until you've stepped back. If you need to hear someone, raise your earmuff volume instead of lifting a cup.
4. When you're done shooting, wash up and wipe down your hearing protection before you eat.
5. On the drive home, notice how your ears feel. If they feel full or sound muffled, your setup needs a better fit or another layer of protection before your next session.
